title: What Qualcomm Has Stopped Leading With
detail:
What Qualcomm Has Stopped Leading With
Trefis Team

AMD
INTC

Image from Pixabay

Qualcomm (QCOM) has spent years telling shareholders it is becoming more than a smartphone chip company. What changed is where the new growth is expected to come from. Two years ago the big non-handset targets were automotive and IoT. Today, the newest leg of the story runs through the data center, and management has already put a number on it.

Qualcomm Once Told You The Laptop Chip Had Redefined Computing

The Snapdragon X Series was the flagship of that older story. Two years ago management said those platforms had redefined personal computing.

Management no longer leads with that story. In the fiscal Q3 2026 call, delivered on July 29, 2026, the PC gets two passing lines: a growing share of design wins in AI-first laptops and Project Solara, a chip-to-cloud platform being built with Microsoft for agent-first enterprise devices. Both are real. Neither carries a revenue figure.

Qualcomm Nearly Doubled Its Non-Handset Target Without Naming The Laptop

Management raised its fiscal 2029 non-handset revenue outlook to $40 billion, up from a previous $22 billion target that covered combined automotive and IoT. The new figure rests on two named legs: more than $24 billion across automotive and IoT, and more than $15 billion in data center. Company revenue over the past twelve months was about $44 billion, so the fiscal 2029 non-handset target alone is close to the whole business today.

Qualcomm calls itself a new entrant in the data center. Two custom silicon wins turn revenue-generating in the December quarter, the opening quarter of a fiscal 2027 in which management forecasts $5 billion of data center revenue. That early revenue, mostly custom chip engagements, comes in significantly below the base business on margin, a drag management sizes at 1.5% to 2% on the weighted average gross margin of QCT, Qualcomm's chip segment.

That reweighting lands while overall growth is soft. Revenue grew 1.9% over the past twelve months against a three-year average pace of 4.8%. QCT gross margins are guided slightly below their historical range on higher input costs, with price increases expected to pull them back up.

You Have Seen Qualcomm Win A New Market Before, In The Car

The counterweight is automotive, and it is already revenue. Fiscal Q3 2026 automotive sales were a record $1.6 billion, up 61% year over year, and management raised the annualized run rate it expects as fiscal 2026 ends to about $7 billion from $6 billion. An expanded BMW agreement made Qualcomm the lead compute silicon provider for that carmaker's next-generation ADAS and digital cockpit.

title: Did You Already Pay For NVIDIA's Bigger Guide?
detail:
Did You Already Pay For NVIDIA's Bigger Guide?
Trefis Team
Wed, September 9, 2026 at 12:16 PM CDT 3 min read

AMD
AVGO
INTC
QCOM
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Photo by analogicus on Pixabay

NVIDIA (NVDA) trades at $225.73, about 4% below its 52-week high after a 35% total return over the past twelve months. Management has just told the market to expect a much larger revenue quarter, and the easy read is that a step that size cannot already be in the price. But the stock's reaction suggests investors have already absorbed much of the news. The question is how much of the revenue step translates into value for shareholders.

What NVIDIA Put On The Table, And What You Paid For It

For fiscal Q3 2027 the company guided revenue to $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%. That is 18.7% above the $91.0 billion it had guided for fiscal Q2 2027, a $17.0 billion step for that one quarter against trailing twelve-month revenue of $302.97 billion. Nothing was revised here. It is a first outlook for a new quarter, set beside the guide for the quarter before.

Across the release, from the $213.05 close before it, to the close after, the stock gained 7.0%, about $14.93 a share. That move paid for the fiscal Q2 2027 results as well as the new guide, so it is not a clean price on the guidance alone.

The $17.0 billion revenue step equates to roughly $0.45 a share at a 63.7% net margin, versus the $14.93 per-share move in the stock. That does not prove the guidance is fully priced in, but it shows why the headline revenue increase alone is not enough to establish upside.

Why NVIDIA's Own Boom Is Raising Its Costs

The squeeze comes from the buildout that fills the order book. Management says pricing conditions in memory are extreme, that the increases have run past what it expected, and that the scarcity is driven in large part by the AI build-out itself. The customers bidding for its systems are bidding up what it pays its memory suppliers.

So the gross margin for fiscal Q3 2027 was guided 0.9 percentage points below the guide given for fiscal Q2 2027. Management expects margin to bottom at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4 2027 before settling at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028, and it guided operating expenses higher in the same release. The volume is guided; the cost of it has just been reset.

What You Actually Own Going Into Fiscal 2028

Management also put a full year on the table for the first time, guiding revenue to grow approximately 70% in fiscal 2028 on what it calls a supply-constrained outlook. That is a far bigger statement than one quarter's step.

Two things carry it. Vera Rubin is shipping in production and is expected to be about 20% of data center revenue in fiscal Q3 2027. ACIE, the sovereign, NeoCloud and enterprise side of the data center business, grew 138% year over year to $40 billion in fiscal Q2 2027. Neither points to a demand problem, and memory is the supply that now sets the margin.

title: AMD Rises 8% in a Month: Should You Buy, Sell or Hold the Stock?
detail:
AMD Rises 8% in a Month: Should You Buy, Sell or Hold the Stock?
Aniruddha Ganguly

Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices AMD shares have risen 7.7% in the past month, outperforming the Zacks Computer and Technology sector's return of 0.7%. The rise reflects growing investor confidence in the company's data-center and AI growth trajectory. AMD shares have outperformed peers, including NVIDIA NVDA, Broadcom AVGO and Intel INTC, over the same time frame. While Broadcom shares have dropped 12.7%, NVIDIA and Intel have returned 3.8% and 7.1%, respectively. So, what should investors do with the AMD shares? Let's find out.

AMD Stock's Price Performance
Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Expanding Data Center Footprint Boosts AMD's Prospects

AMD's expanding Data Center footprint (58% of second-quarter 2026 revenues) is driven by strong demand for EPYC server CPUs. In the second quarter of 2026, Data Center revenues jumped 107% year over year to $6.7 billion, supported by robust EPYC processor demand and the continued ramp of Instinct GPUs. AMD expects the Data Center business to more than double in 2027, while server CPU revenues are projected to increase more than 80% year over year in the second half of 2026 and more than 70% in 2027. The company also indicated that inference is overtaking training as a major source of AI compute demand, while agentic AI is creating incremental demand for both GPUs and CPUs.

Increasing confidence in the Helios and MI450 ramp is a catalyst for the company. AMD expects initial production shipments in the third quarter, followed by a significant step-up in the fourth quarter and another increase in the first quarter of 2027. Demand for 2027 has moved above AMD's initial expectations. Helios combines MI450-series GPUs, EPYC CPUs, Pensando networking and ROCm software, while strategic relationships with OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic provide substantial visibility into multi-generation, gigawatt-scale deployments.

The Helios and Instinct roadmap should remain a major growth engine beyond 2026. AMD intends to introduce a new rack-scale AI platform every year. Following the MI450-based Helios platform, its next-generation platform is expected to combine MI500-series GPUs, Verano CPUs and Pensando networking. Customer engagement around MI500 is already strong. Longer-term engineering relationships with OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic are also influencing future MI500, MI600 and rack architectures, improving AMD's visibility across multiple generations of AI deployments.

Moreover, improving visibility into AMD's server CPU franchise. EPYC deployments continue to broaden across hyperscalers and enterprises, while sixth-generation EPYC Venice is expected to extend AMD's performance and efficiency advantages. Customer demand for Venice is stronger than for any previous EPYC generation, according to management. AMD has also been increasing wafer, packaging and other supply-chain capacity to capture the accelerating demand environment. AMD estimates the server CPU market could exceed $220 billion by 2030, with agentic AI workloads becoming a major portion of the opportunity.

AI infrastructure represents AMD's most important long-term growth opportunity. AMD expects the data-center AI accelerator market to reach roughly $1.4 trillion by 2030, while the server CPU opportunity is expected to reach approximately $220 billion. The company believes its broader compute portfolio spanning GPUs, CPUs, networking, adaptive compute and software should enable it to participate across multiple layers of this expanding AI infrastructure market.

title: Should You Buy Intel Stock Because The Comeback Is Working?

Should You Buy Intel Stock Because The Comeback Is Working?

Image from Pixabay

Intel (INTC) has been repriced as a comeback over the past year, and the products are cooperating. Revenue reached $16.1 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up 25% from a year earlier, while trailing-twelve-month revenue was up 7.5% to $57.0 billion. The server line is supply-constrained. The harder question is what your money buys at this price.

Why Is Intel Growing Again?

The growth sits in one place. Intel's data center and AI group brought in $6.3 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up 59% from a year earlier, and Xeon 6 is one of the fastest-ramping products in the company's history. Demand keeps outrunning supply, by management's account, with the industry short of wafers, memory, and substrates.

The client side contributed $8.9 billion, but management said the market remains softer and expects the business to be down year over year. Both product groups make money. The client group turned 26% of its second-quarter revenue into operating profit, the data center group 40%. The product businesses are profitable, but the comeback is being driven primarily by data centers and AI.

Where Does Intel's Product Profit Go?

Into the factories. Intel Foundry took in $5.8 billion in the second quarter of 2026, nearly all of it from Intel itself, and lost $2.1 billion doing it, $348 million less than the quarter before. Only $293 million came from outside customers. The foundry is still an expensive internal supplier.

So the company numbers look nothing like the segment ones. The trailing twelve-month operating margin is 7.6% against 18.6% for the S&P 500, and Intel still posted a net loss of $11.3 billion over those twelve months. There is no earnings multiple to argue about. What you pay is 9.3 times sales, against 3.2 for the index.

Closing that profit gap is not Intel's call alone. It depends on outside chip designers picking its fabs, and the pitch to them rests on 14A. The company's own timetable puts risk production for internal products in the second half of 2027 and a committed high-volume ramp in 2028. Capital spending runs to more than $20 billion for 2026, with 2027 guided higher again.

You Are Paying For The Fabs Either Way

The stock has already run. Intel has returned 327% over the trailing twelve months, has given back 5% over the trailing three months, and sits about 26% below its 52-week high. When markets last broke, in the 2022 inflation shock, Intel fell 52% against 24% for the S&P 500.

Shareholders have already been asked for more. In August 2026 Intel priced $20 billion of new stock at $95 a share, and it trades near $104.50 now. Debt is 9.5% of market value, so the balance sheet is not the pressure point. Dilution and the capital bill are.

title: NVDA Stock Is Running. Is There Fuel Left?
detail:
NVDA Stock Is Running. Is There Fuel Left?
Trefis Team

MRVL

AVGO
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Image from Pixabay

This chipmaker's stock has been on a historic tear, but for investors arriving now, the critical question is whether the business can still outrun its already premium price.

NVIDIA (NVDA) builds the engines of the artificial intelligence revolution, from the chips to the full-stack systems that function as complete "AI factories." The market has rewarded this position handsomely, bidding the stock up 35% over the last twelve months. It now sits as the most valuable company tracked by Trefis. The run is real, ranking in the top 38% of large US stocks on trend strength. The open question for any would-be buyer is whether the price already charges for all of it. Is this momentum with fuel, or momentum fully priced?

Is A Real Business Powering This Run?

The numbers show an engine running at full throttle. Over the last twelve months, NVIDIA's revenue grew 83%, a different order of magnitude from the S&P 500 median of 8.4%. The company translates this top-line growth into immense profitability. The company's operating margin is 65%, crushing the 18.6% median for the index.

This performance is rooted in a surge in AI demand for its integrated platforms. The company is capturing more value with each generation, with management noting its revenue opportunity has grown from roughly $18 billion per gigawatt with its Hopper platform to $40 billion with the new Vera Rubin platform. Growth is also diversifying. While hyperscale cloud providers remain key, management states that its ACIE segment, which includes sovereign AI, regional NeoClouds, and enterprises, will represent roughly half of its data center business.

What Does a Ticket Cost, and What Is the Catch?

An investor today pays a premium for that quality. The stock trades at a price-to-earnings multiple of 28.3, above the S&P 500 median of 23.0. Its price-to-sales multiple of 18.0 is also significantly richer than the median of 3.2. While the stock has been a strong performer, it currently trades about 4% below its 52-week high.

The real catch, however, is a business risk, not a valuation metric. To fuel the ecosystem, management has invested nearly $50 billion in the so-called Frontier AI labs. While this supports major customers, it has also raised questions about what some call "circular financing." The risk is that NVIDIA is using its own balance sheet to fund customers who, in turn, are developing their own custom chips that could one day compete. It's a strategic gamble that the ecosystem built on its CUDA platform will prove more valuable than the risk of nurturing future rivals. For investors looking at other ways to participate in this space, a semiconductor ETF like SOXQ offers broader exposure.

title: Should You Buy Intel Stock After a Nearly Fourfold Year?
detail:
Should You Buy Intel Stock After a Nearly Fourfold Year?
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Wed, September 9, 2026 at 3:07 AM CDT 5 min read
INTC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Two things at Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) have nearly quadrupled over the past 12 months. One is the quarterly operating income of the chipmaker's data center business. The other is its stock price, which trades near $96 as of this writing, up from a 52-week low of $24.05 and about a third below the high of $142.35 it set in late June.

The rally has lifted Intel's market value to about $500 billion -- this for a company that lost $11 billion on paper in its most recent quarter. And the price is about 47 times what analysts think the company can earn next year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The business is improving faster than it has in years. I just don't think it has improved as fast as the price.

Image source: Intel.

The data center business earned the rally

Intel's second-quarter revenue of $16.1 billion was up 25% year over year -- growth CEO Lip-Bu Tan called the company's strongest in more than 15 years.

No part of the company improved more than the data center and artificial intelligence (AI) segment. A year ago, the segment earned $633 million of operating income in a quarter. In the first quarter of 2026, it earned $1.5 billion. And in the second quarter, the figure reached $2.5 billion. Revenue growth is accelerating as well, from 22% in the first quarter to 59% in the second.

Management said the quarter's server growth was the strongest on record. The segment's operating margin, meanwhile, now sits at about 40%.

Companywide, adjusted earnings per share swung from a year-ago loss of $0.10 to a profit of $0.42.

The $11 billion net loss Intel reported for the period, meanwhile, traces to a $12.5 billion noncash charge tied to shares held in escrow for the U.S. government, which took a stake in the company last year. Cash from operations during the quarter was $7 billion.

Is the foundry fixed?

Not yet -- but it is losing money more slowly. Intel Foundry's second-quarter revenue grew 31% year over year to $5.8 billion, and it still lost $2.1 billion at the operating line, an improvement from $3.2 billion in the same period last year. First-half losses total $4.5 billion, down from $5.5 billion a year earlier.

Nearly all of that revenue, however, still comes from Intel buying from itself. Customers outside the company accounted for just $293 million in the period, compared with $22 million in the same quarter of 2025. That leaves external sales at less than 2% of Intel's total revenue.
